claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The relatively low hardness and strength arise from a near-ideal atomic mixture with minimal lattice distortion.
The simple solid solution contains few intrinsic obstacles to dislocation motion and therefore has low solid-solution strengthening.
Low dislocation pinning promotes plasticity and machinability at the expense of hardness and strength.
Secondary phases or departures from equimolar composition can strengthen similar HEAs through increased lattice distortion or precipitation hardening.
The starting material is as-cast equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase disordered solid-solution state.
Controlled aging can induce nanoscale secondary precipitates that increase lattice distortion and dislocation pinning.
A modest increase in Ti or another constituent can increase lattice mismatch in CoCrFeNiTi.
Balanced atomic sizes and mixing enthalpies in the simple solid solution produce low friction stress for dislocation motion.
Increased lattice distortion or dispersed nanoscale precipitates obstruct dislocation glide and increase dislocation pinning.
Obstructing dislocation glide raises hardness and strength while reducing ductility.
The intervention is predicted to increase hardness and compressive yield strength by approximately 15–30% relative to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The predicted increase in hardness and compressive yield strength will be accompanied by reduced ductility.
Unmodified equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has moderate hardness and strength but high plasticity and ease of machining because of low dislocation resistance.
The proposed mechanism is limited to room-temperature testing, comparable grain sizes, and thermal histories that avoid uncontrolled phase transformation, coarse segregation, or embrittlement.
Failure to observe increased hardness and compressive strength, decreased ductility, and evidence of increased lattice distortion or secondary phases would reject the proposed explanation.

contradictions.description: The aging intervention is intended to create secondary precipitates, whereas the boundary states that specimens should be maintained in a single-phase state.

The intervention intentionally changes phase constitution or composition, while the conditions call for the overall microstructure to remain constant; only non-target variables such as grain size could realistically be held constant.
The intervention includes a composition-adjustment branch, but the experimental design describes both sample sets as having the same base composition.
